title: PROVERBS LITERALLY TELLS A HUSBAND TO BE “INTOXICATED” WITH HIS WIFE’S LOVE
paragraphs: PROVERBS LITERALLY TELLS A HUSBAND TO BE “INTOXICATED” WITH HIS WIFE’S LOVE
Maybe the Bible’s answer to temptation is more beautiful—and more intimate—than many Christians were ever taught.
There is a sentence in Proverbs that sounds almost too passionate to be sitting inside the Bible.
Not because it is vulgar.
Because it is breathtakingly unashamed.
God does not merely tell a husband, “Do not commit adultery.”
He gives him something far more beautiful to pursue.
“Rejoice in the wife of your youth.”
And then Scripture goes further.
Much further.
The Hebrew of Proverbs 5:19 ends with these words:
בְּאַהֲבָתָהּ תִּשְׁגֶּה תָמִיד
Be’ahavatah tishgeh tamid.
A close rendering is:
“In her love, be intoxicated continually.”
Read that again.
Not intoxicated with another woman.
Not intoxicated with pornography.
Not intoxicated with fantasy.
Not intoxicated with the endless parade of carefully edited bodies glowing from a screen.
Not intoxicated with the attention of someone who is not your spouse.
With her.
Your wife.
The woman whose face you have seen exhausted.
The woman whose imperfections you know.
The woman who has seen yours.

The woman who may have stood beside you through bills, children, disappointment, arguments, sickness, aging, ordinary Tuesdays, unanswered prayers, and seasons when neither of you felt particularly romantic.
Scripture says something astonishing:
Keep finding your way back to her.

The Hebrew verb behind that startling statement is שָׁגָה — shagah. In this context it carries the imagery of being so captivated that one reels—as though intoxicated. That is why faithful English translations variously render the expression “intoxicated,” “captivated,” “exhilarated,” “enraptured,” or “lost” in her love.
This is not a mistranslation designed to make Scripture provocative.
The Hebrew really is that vivid.
And that matters.
Because some Christians were accidentally taught a version of holiness in which marriage is permitted but passion is suspicious.
Sexual desire became something Christians whispered about.
Bodies became embarrassing.
Romance became something tolerated before marriage and forgotten afterward.
And holiness somehow became synonymous with emotional coldness.
But Proverbs 5 will not allow that distortion.
God created marital intimacy.
And within the covenant of marriage, Scripture does not merely tolerate delight.
It celebrates it.
Proverbs 5:18–19 speaks of a blessed fountain, rejoicing in “the wife of your youth,” satisfaction within marriage, and continuing captivation by her love.
That is not pornography wearing religious clothing.
It is covenant poetry.
There is an enormous difference.
Pornography teaches you to consume bodies.
Covenant teaches you to cherish a person.
Lust says, “What can you give me?”
Love says, “How can I faithfully give myself to you?”
Pornography trains the eyes to wander.
Covenant calls the eyes home.
Adultery requires secrecy.
Biblical marriage invites nakedness without shame, faithfulness without divided loyalties, and intimacy without the terror that someone will disappear when pleasure stops being convenient.
And here is what makes Proverbs 5 even more powerful.
You cannot understand verse 19 if you rip it out of the chapter and turn it into a romantic slogan.
The chapter is a warning.

A father is teaching his son about sexual temptation. Forbidden desire initially tastes sweet, but the path eventually becomes bitter. The young man is warned not to surrender his strength, dignity, years, and life to sexual unfaithfulness.
Then, in the middle of that warning, Scripture does something beautiful.
It does not merely say:
Stay away.
It essentially says:
Come home.
Drink from your own well.
Rejoice in your wife.
Delight in her.
Remain captivated by her love.
That is a radically different picture of sexual holiness.
Holiness is not merely saying no to forbidden desire.
It is learning to say a wholehearted yes to what God has called good.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs to hear that before another marriage quietly freezes to death.
Your spouse should not have to compete with an imaginary woman who does not exist.
She should not have to compete with pornography.
She should not have to compete with your memories of somebody from twenty years ago.

She should not have to compete with filtered faces, curated bodies, private messages, flirtatious coworkers, secret accounts, or the fantasy that somewhere there is a person who would give you pleasure without ever requiring patience, sacrifice, forgiveness, responsibility, or covenant.
Fantasy is easy precisely because fantasy never asks you to love a real human being.
Marriage does.
Marriage eventually introduces you to morning breath and medical appointments.
Laundry.
Misunderstandings.
Financial pressure.
Stretch marks.
Scars.
Gray hair.
Children crying at 2:17 in the morning.
Seasons of grief.
Seasons of exhaustion.
Moments when affection feels effortless.
Moments when choosing love feels like carrying a cross.
And somewhere inside all of that ordinary humanity, God says:
Rejoice in the wife of your youth.
That command becomes more beautiful the longer you sit with it.
Because the “wife of your youth” eventually stops being young.
So do you.
The hands change.
The face changes.
The body changes.
Life writes its history across both of you.
But covenant says:
I am still here.
I still see you.
I still choose you.
I will not train my heart to despise what time has touched.
I will not demand that the woman beside me compete with twenty-year-olds manufactured by algorithms for my attention.
I will remember the person beneath the changing body.
I will remember the promises.
I will remember the laughter.
I will remember the nights we almost broke.
I will remember the prayers nobody else heard.
I will remember the battles we survived.
And by the grace of God, I will keep learning how to delight in you.
That is far more powerful than lust.
Lust requires novelty.
Covenant discovers depth.
Lust becomes bored because it keeps asking for another body.
Love keeps discovering the mystery of the same person.
And perhaps this is where the verse stops being beautiful and starts becoming painful.
Because some husbands reading this know exactly where their affection has gone.
Some wives know exactly what it feels like to lie beside a man whose body is in the room but whose desire lives somewhere else.
Some husbands know what it is to have allowed resentment to turn tenderness into distance.
Some marriages have not experienced affection in months.
Some in years.
Some people reading these words have hidden browser histories.
Hidden conversations.
Hidden fantasies.
Hidden affairs.
Hidden wounds.
And Christianity does not heal us by teaching us to hide better.
Jesus brings hidden things into the light.
Not so sinners can be publicly humiliated.
So sinners can be redeemed.
That is the scandal of grace.
Jesus Christ did not come for people who had successfully made themselves spotless.
He came to save sinners.
The Gospel does not say, “Clean yourself until Jesus can tolerate you.”
The Gospel announces that Christ died for sinners, rose again, calls us to repentance, and offers forgiveness and new life to those who come to Him.
Grace is not God pretending sin does not matter.
Look at the cross.
Sin mattered enough for Christ to bleed.
But look at the cross again.
You mattered enough for Him to bleed.
So if pornography has poisoned your marriage, bring it into the light.
If adultery has shattered trust, stop baptizing deception with excuses.
If flirtation has become emotional infidelity, stop calling it friendship simply because nobody has touched yet.
If bitterness has made you emotionally abandon your spouse, confess it.
If you have used Proverbs 5 as permission to demand intimacy while refusing tenderness, repentance belongs there too.
Because Proverbs 5:19 is not a divine authorization for husbands to treat wives as objects.
Quite the opposite.
The woman in the passage is not pornography with a wedding ring.
She is “the wife of your youth.”
A covenant partner.
A person to rejoice in.
A person whose love is treasured.
Biblical marital intimacy cannot be separated from the broader commands of Christlike love, faithfulness, honor, sacrifice, kindness, patience, forgiveness, and mutual care.
A husband following Jesus cannot demand that his wife become an instrument for his appetite while he ignores her heart.
Christ does not teach men to consume women.
He teaches His people sacrificial love.
Ephesians 5 points husbands toward the staggering standard of Christ’s love for the church—a love characterized by self-giving sacrifice.
That changes everything.
A Christian husband does not ask only:
“Does my wife satisfy me?”
He must also ask:
“Does she feel cherished by me?”
“Does she feel safe with me?”
“Have I listened to her?”
“Have I prayed for her?”
“Have I wounded her and refused to apologize?”
“Have I spent more energy pursuing strangers on a screen than pursuing the woman I promised before God to love?”
That last question may hurt.
Let it.
Sometimes conviction is mercy knocking before destruction kicks the door down.

And wives are not outside the call to covenant faithfulness either. Christian marriage calls both husband and wife away from contempt, manipulation, infidelity, cruelty, indifference, and selfishness and toward faithful, Christ-shaped love.
This is not about pretending every troubled marriage can be repaired with a romantic dinner.
Some marriages carry profound betrayal.

Some involve abuse, coercion, danger, or serious patterns requiring wise pastoral, professional, or legal help. Scripture's celebration of marital intimacy must never be weaponized to pressure someone into sexual activity or silence someone who is unsafe.
Biblical love never needs abuse to survive.
But where repentance is real, where safety is present, where two wounded people are willing to submit themselves to Christ, grace can begin doing what human pride said was impossible.
Slowly.
Sometimes painfully.
Trust may return one honest conversation at a time.
Tenderness may return one gentle touch at a time.
Prayer may return awkwardly.
Forgiveness may involve tears.
A marriage may have to learn how to speak again before it learns how to laugh again.
And that is okay.
Restoration does not always look dramatic.
Sometimes resurrection begins with two people sitting at the kitchen table saying:
“We cannot keep living like this.”
Then one of them whispers:
“I'm sorry.”
And the other starts crying.
And somewhere unseen, grace enters the room.
Maybe that is you.
Maybe your marriage is beautiful right now.
Protect it.
Maybe it is tired.
Nourish it.
Maybe it is wounded.
Seek help and bring the truth into the light.
Maybe you are single.

Then do not read Proverbs 5 as permission to awaken covenant privileges outside covenant. Let it teach you that biblical sexuality is not dirty, but neither is it casual. God's vision connects sexual delight with faithfulness rather than separating pleasure from responsibility.
Maybe you have already failed sexually.
Then hear this carefully:
Your failure does not outrun the blood of Jesus Christ.
Repentance is not pretending it never happened.
Grace is not permission to continue.
The Gospel gives something far better.
Forgiveness.
Cleansing.
A new direction.
A transformed heart.
You may carry consequences.
Trust may need rebuilding.
Relationships may not instantly return to what they were.
But the cross means your worst chapter does not have to become the title of your entire life.
Peter had chapters he wished he could erase.
The woman at the well had chapters.
The woman caught in adultery had chapters.
David had horrifying chapters.
The church at Corinth was filled with people who had chapters.
And then Jesus entered the story.
That is why Gospel Warrior keeps returning to this truth:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By redeeming sinners in the middle of it.
Maybe the greatest miracle your marriage needs is not for your spouse to become somebody different.
Maybe you need Jesus to change the way you see the person already beside you.
To give you eyes that stop wandering.
A heart that stops comparing.
Hands that learn tenderness again.
A mouth that speaks life instead of contempt.
Humility that knows how to apologize without adding, “but you…”
Courage to confess what has been hidden.
Strength to delete what needs deleting.
Wisdom to establish boundaries.
Grace to forgive.
Patience to rebuild.
And love that says:
After everything...
I want to learn you again.
Maybe tonight the holiest thing some married couple can do is put the phones down.
Sit beside each other.
Look at each other.
Not as roommates.
Not as coworkers managing children.
Not as two exhausted people sharing expenses.
As husband and wife.
And say:
“Where did we lose each other?”
Then listen.
Really listen.
And if the answer hurts, do not run immediately.
Bring Jesus into the wound.
Because the same Christ who forgives sinners can teach forgiven sinners how to love.
And perhaps now Proverbs 5:19 does not sound scandalous anymore.
Perhaps it sounds like rescue.
בְּאַהֲבָתָהּ תִּשְׁגֶּה תָמִיד
Be’ahavatah tishgeh tamid.
Be continually captivated by her love.
Come home.
Following Gospel Warrior keeps Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, and discipleship appearing in a feed designed to pull your attention in a thousand other directions.
Supporting Gospel work through sharing and voluntary financial support can be one way believers choose to steward resources for ministry; it should never be confused with earning God's favor.
Because Christianity's message is not that righteous people never become dirty.
It is that Jesus Christ still washes sinners who come to Him.
And maybe years from now, the greatest love story in your house will not be that two people never broke each other's hearts.
It will be that when everything seemed too broken to rewrite, Jesus picked up the pen.
